# Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman, born on March 16, 1953 in New York City to a Jewish family, developed a deep interest in computers from a young age, working on programming projects during his high school years. He attended Harvard University, excelling in mathematics, before joining the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory where he became a pivotal figure in the hacker community. Stallman’s early work included contributions to software like TECO and Emacs and development in AI backtracking algorithms. His experiences with software restrictions and proprietary licensing in the late 1970s led him to champion software freedom.
In 1983, Stallman launched the GNU Project, aimed at creating a free Unix-compatible operating system. He also founded the Free Software Foundation to support this goal and popularized the concept of copyleft to protect software freedoms. Stallman developed crucial tools such as GNU Emacs, GCC, and GDB; however, the Linux kernel developed by Linus Torvalds became the foundation for widespread adoption of GNU/Linux systems. Stallman is well known for his staunch political activism for free software, maintaining strict stances on terminology and ethics in software freedom. After controversies related to comments on sensitive topics in 2019, he resigned from MIT and the FSF but returned to the FSF board in 2021, a move that elicited mixed reactions from the free software community. Stallman continues to promote software freedom and live according to his principles, including extensive measures to protect personal privacy and surveillance resistance. He has received numerous honors, including the MacArthur Fellowship and membership in the US National Academy of Engineering.
